notes.title: 아이고
notes.text: 아이고 is the all-purpose Korean sigh: pain (아이고, 아파!), surprise, tiredness, even joy. Older people say it all the time. 아야! is a sharper "ouch!". When someone gets hurt, ask politely: 많이 다치셨어요? (Are you badly hurt?)

notes.title: Korean clinics
notes.text: Most Koreans go straight to a specialist clinic instead of a family doctor: 정형외과 (bones and joints), 내과 (internal medicine), 이비인후과 (ear, nose and throat), 치과 (dentist). National health insurance (건강 보험) keeps visits cheap and waits short.

notes.title: Honorific care words
notes.text: With elders, everyday verbs change: 자다 → 주무시다 (sleep), 먹다 → 드시다 (eat), 있다 → 계시다 (stay). 모시다 means "to take care of or accompany an elder" — 부모님을 모시고 살아요 "I live with and look after my parents."

notes.title: 몸살
notes.text: 몸살 is the achy, wiped-out, feverish feeling after overwork or a cold — a very Korean word. 몸살 났어요 is a perfectly good reason to stay home. Folk remedies: rest, warm 생강차 (ginger tea), 유자차 (citron tea), or honey-lemon tea.

notes.title: 머리 vs 머리카락
notes.text: 머리 means both "head" and "hair" in daily speech (머리를 잘랐어요 = I got a haircut). 머리카락 is a strand or strands of hair specifically. 뺨 and 볼 both mean "cheek"; kids' songs use 볼, and 뺨 appears in expressions like 뺨을 맞다 (to get slapped).
